name: Pendant
description: A pendant lamp from the 1970s, constructed from brass and translucent mother-of-pearl shell. The shade has a wide trumpet-shaped profile with a narrow upper neck and broad flaring lower edge. Thin brass elements form a gridded structure, holding the individual shell panels in place and giving the lamp its clear architectural rhythm. The use of mother-of-pearl shell gives the pendant a warm, diffused quality when lit. Seen from below, the shade reveals a concentric pattern of shell segments, creating a geometric mosaic that follows the curve of the form.

name: A pair of 'Struten' ceiling lamps designed by Hans Bergström, for Atelje Lyktan
description: Hans Bergström’s Struten (Model 181) is an iconic pendant lamp that exemplifies the essence of mid-20th-century Scandinavian design. Launched in the 1950s and manufactured by Ateljé Lyktan, the lamp is defined by its sleek, conical form in white acrylic plastic, showcasing Bergström’s dedication to modern simplicity and refined aesthetics. Also known as "the cone," Struten earned a gold medal at the 1950 Milan Triennale and is widely regarded as one of Bergström’s most effortlessly stylish and well-balanced creations. A pivotal figure in Swedish design, Hans Bergström (1910–1996) made a lasting impact on lighting throughout the 20th century. In 1934, he and his wife, Verna Norell, established Ateljé Lyktan in Helsingborg, shaping the company into a key force in Scandinavian lighting innovation.

name: Ceiling lamp model 6022 designed by Gunnar Asplund
description: The model was originally created for Gunnar Asplund's music room at the Workshop's exhibition held at Liljevalchs Konsthall in autumn 1920. It became part of Böhlmark's collection in 1922 and remained so until Ateljé Lyktan took over production in 1965. The lamp features a green lacquered metal suspension, with three delicate chains descending to support the gently curved matt opal glass shade. The design is simple yet refined, perfectly balancing functionality with an artistic, decorative quality. Gunnar Asplund (1885–1940) was a pioneering Swedish architect and designer, widely regarded as one of the key figures in Nordic Classicism and the transition to Functionalism in Scandinavian architecture. His work combined classical influences with modernist principles, leaving a profound and lasting impact on Swedish design and architecture. Pieces like the Ceiling Lamp Model 6022 demonstrate his ability to merge decorative flourishes with modernist simplicity, reflecting his attention to detail and functional elegance.

name: Ceiling lamp designed by by Palle Suenson
description: Palle Suenson was one of the leading Danish architects of the twentieth century. His style balanced impressive scale and form, always elevated by scrupulous artistic attention to detail and materials. Many of Denmark’s renowned furniture designers, including Hans Wegner and Poul Kjaerholm worked under Palle Suenson during their early careers.

name: Ceiling lamp
description: This ceiling lamp is a refined example of Swedish Grace from the 1930s, characterised by its restrained form enriched with decorative detail. The fixture is composed of a circular disc of green-toned glass, often referred to as råglas , etched with stylised stork motifs arranged in a rhythmic, symmetrical composition. The lamp reflects the distinct character of Swedish Grace, a Nordic interpretation of Art Deco that favoured clarity of form combined with carefully applied ornament. Rather than fully integrated sculptural decoration, motifs such as birds or classical figures were often used as surface embellishment. Swedish Grace gained international recognition following Sweden’s success at the 1925 Paris Exposition, where the style established itself as a hallmark of Swedish design.

name: Ceiling lamp designed by Carl-Harry Stålhane for Rörstrand
description: Designed in the 1950s by Carl-Harry Stålhane for Rörstrand, this ceiling lamp illustrates how ceramic craftsmanship was thoughtfully translated into modern lighting. The tapered shade is produced in white feldspar porcelain and defined by a finely modelled geometric relief. During this period, Stålhane’s stoneware was shaped by gently classical forms with clear references to Chinese ceramic traditions. Stålhane joined Rörstrand at a young age and remained closely associated with the factory for more than three decades, eventually succeeding Gunnar Nylund as artistic director. His work from this period is marked by a balance between classical restraint and modern expression, drawing on historical references while remaining firmly rooted in mid-century design thinking. His work is held in major international collections, including the Swedish National Museum of Art and Design in Stockholm and the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

name: Ceiling lamp designed by Carl Fagerlund for Orrefors
description: Designed by Carl Fagerlund for Orrefors in the 1960s, this ceiling lamp is a substantial example of Swedish glass lighting from the post-war period. The fixture is constructed around a brass framework that supports two concentric layers of circular glass cups. Arranged with precision, the glass elements soften and diffuse the light while shielding the eye from direct glare, creating an even and controlled illumination. The thick, moulded glass reflects Fagerlund’s distinctive approach to lighting design, in which material weight and optical clarity are carefully balanced. Carl Fagerlund was Orrefors’ most influential lighting designer, instrumental in the company’s expansion beyond traditional crystal objects into architectural lighting. Founded in 1898, Orrefors was a central figure in Nordic glass production throughout the 20th century and Fagerlund’s lamps remain among its most recognisable designs. This piece exemplifies his ability to merge refined craftsmanship with a clear understanding of light and space.

name: Ceiling lamp designed by Helger Johansson for Westal
description: Designed in the 1960s by Holger Johansson for Westal, this ceiling lamp is a refined example of Swedish mid-century lighting that balances structure, material and atmosphere. The composition centres on a geometric brass framework from which multiple smoked glass shades are evenly suspended, creating a calm, architectural rhythm while softening the light through the tinted glass. Holger Johansson (1926–2015) was a central figure in Swedish lighting design and the founder of Westal, which he established in 1947 under the name Habo Elarmaturer. Johansson became particularly recognised for ceiling lamps of this type. By the late 1960s, the company’s success required expansion, leading to the construction of a new, purpose-built factory in Bankeryd in 1968—a facility that continues to house Westal today.

name: Ceiling lamp designed by Hans-Agne Jakobsson
description: Active between the 1950s and 1970s—in the golden age of Scandinavian design—Swedish interior decorator and furniture designer Hans-Agne Jakobsson is best remembered for his softly glowing, glare-free lighting fixtures, which were inspired by the "organic modern" approaches of Danish lighting master Poul Henningsen and Finnish icon Alvar Aalto. Experimenting with a wide range of materials—including brass, iron, glass, fabric, and wood shavings—Jakobsson mastered both the direction and colour of light. His designs are known for their hidden bulbs and streamlined ornamentation, which created diffused, muted lighting. A prolific career to say the least, his company produced over 2,000 separate Hans-Agne Jakobsson lamp designs.

name: Ceiling lamp designed by Alvar Aalto for Idman
description: This ceiling lamp, designed by Alvar Aalto for the Finnish lighting manufacturer Idman in the 1950s, was originally developed for the Stora Enso head office in Helsinki, a landmark building completed in 1962 and designed by Aalto as a total work of art, from façade to interior details. It is a restrained yet highly considered example of his approach to architectural lighting. Composed in white-lacquered metal, the lamp is defined by a layered internal structure that softens and controls the light, preventing glare while creating an even, ambient glow, reflecting Aalto’s belief that light should support both comfort and concentration. Alvar Aalto (1898–1976) worked across architecture, furniture, lighting, and glass, always treating these disciplines as interconnected. Emerging from a Functionalist foundation that brought him international recognition in the early 1930s, he developed a more humane modernism rooted in user-friendly design and careful material choices. His lighting designs, like this example, combine technical clarity with an intuitive understanding of space, contributing to his enduring influence on modern design. Marked.

name: Set of three ceiling lamps/chandeliers
Ceiling lamp ‘PH Louvre’ designed by Poul Henningsen for Louis Poulsen
description: The PH Louvre ceiling lamp was designed in 1957 by Poul Henningsen for Louis Poulsen. It was created specifically for the Adventist Church at Skodsborg Badesanatorium, Denmark. This chandelier is the original fixture installed in the church, retaining a direct and documented connection to its original architectural setting. Developed within an architectural context associated with Charles K. Gjerrild, the PH Louvre reflects Henningsen’s aim to provide economical lighting suitable for a church interior while maintaining a high quality of light. The PH Louvre is related to an earlier design by Henningsen known as The Spiral (1942), which offered similar lighting principles but was more complex and costly to manufacture. The PH Louvre, sometimes referred to as the “Bullet Lamp,” represents a simplified and more economical development of these ideas. The PH Louvre consists of 13 concentric, horizontally arranged shades mounted around a central structure. These elements are precisely proportioned and spaced to shield the light source from direct view while reflecting light downward and outward, producing an even and comfortable illumination with minimal glare. The example presented here has a diameter of 60 cm and a copper-coloured finish. Henningsen developed the foundations of his lighting system in the mid-1920s, beginning with the three-shade system presented at the 1925 Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes in Paris. His collaboration with Louis Poulsen continued uninterrupted until his death in 1967, during which he consistently focused on controlling light through reflection and shielding to eliminate glare and create soft, readable illumination.

name: Pendant/table lamp 'Nippon' designed by Simon P. Henningsen for Lyfa
description: Designed by Simon P. Henningsen for Lyfa in the 1970s, the 'Nippon' lamp is constructed from folded, lacquered metal sheets arranged in a strict rectangular form. A vertical red band and an internal orange disc introduce colour and depth, with the orange disc deliberately positioned to soften the light and cast a warm glow. The name ’Nippon,’ the Japanese word for Japan, refers directly to the lamp’s internal orange disc, conceived by Henningsen as a setting sun. The lamp is designed to function either as a pendant or as a standing table lamp, reflecting a deliberate emphasis on adaptability and economical production. Simon P. Henningsen approached lighting as both a technical and expressive discipline, often working with bold geometry, colour, and reflective surfaces. The son of Poul Henningsen, he was deeply influenced by lighting theory from an early age and later succeeded his father as chief architect of Tivoli Gardens in Copenhagen.

name: Ceiling lamp model A335B designed by Alvar Aalto for Valaistustyö
description: Designed by Alvar Aalto for the Finnish manufacturer Valaistustyö, the 'A335B' ceiling lamp is a distinctive example of his later lighting work. Formed in pressed metal, the lamp is defined by its domed silhouette and the characteristic perforated lower section, which allows light to escape downward in a controlled and rhythmic pattern while maintaining a soft overall glow. This careful modulation of light reflects Aalto’s enduring interest in how illumination shapes atmosphere and supports everyday use. Compact yet expressive, the 'A335B' was conceived as a functional object with a strong architectural presence, equally suited to domestic and public interiors. No longer in production, the model has become increasingly scarce and is represented in the collections of the Alvar Aalto Museum, underscoring its significance within his body of work. As with much of Aalto’s design, the 'A335B' embodies his holistic approach, where lighting, furniture and architecture were conceived as interconnected elements, united by a commitment to human-centred design, clarity of form and thoughtful material use. Stamped

name: Ceiling lamp designed by Lisa Johansson-Pape,
Long ceiling lamps designed by Hans Agne Jakobsson
description: Designed by Hans Agne Jakobsson, these long ceiling lamps are a distilled expression of Scandinavian lighting from the mid-20th century. Executed in brass and glass, the lamps reflect Jakobsson’s broader material experimentation and his belief that lighting should enhance atmosphere rather than dominate it. Jakobsson was active during the golden age of Scandinavian design from the 1950s through the 1970s and became known for his sensitive handling of illumination. Influenced by the glare-free principles developed by designers such as Poul Henningsen and Alvar Aalto, he focused on controlling both the direction and warmth of light. While many of his designs employ layered shades, these pendant lamps instead rely on clarity and restraint, producing an open, ambient glow that integrates seamlessly into modern interiors.

name: Ceiling lamp PH 4/4 designed by Poul Henningsen for Louis Poulsen
description: Poul Henningsen developed an extensive body of lighting designs built around his pioneering three-shade principle, first introduced in 1926. This system was conceived to produce controlled, glare-free illumination by directing light precisely where it was needed. Many of his lamps are identified by numerical designations that refer directly to the diameter of the individual shades, making the proportions and light distribution an integral part of each model’s identity. The PH 4/4 pendant belongs to what Henningsen regarded as the full-scale versions of his lighting programme. With a top shade measuring around 40 cm in diameter, it maintains the carefully calculated 3:2:1 relationship between the upper, middle, and lower shades. This proportional balance results in a soft, even light that feels generous yet contained, characteristic of Henningsen’s most successful designs. Central to Henningsen’s approach was a rigorous consideration of materials and surface treatments, all selected to minimise glare and unwanted shadow. From the late 1920s onwards, he increasingly worked with combinations such as opal glass and copper, refining both the technical performance and the visual expression of his lamps. The result was a lighting system in which form, material and light quality were inseparable, setting a lasting standard for modern lighting design. Stamped.

name: Pair of ceiling lamps
Ceiling lamp 'Garbo' designed by Mariyo Yagi for Sirrah
description: Designed by Mariyo Yagi in collaboration with Studio Simon and produced by Sirrah in the 1970s, the 'Garbo' ceiling lamp is a unique sculptural lighting piece. Suspended from a discreet metal ceiling mount, fine braided nylon cords descend in dense vertical strands, forming a luminous curtain that softly diffuses the light from within. When illuminated, the fringe creates a shifting play of shadow and transparency. The design is rooted in Yagi’s concept of Nawa , a philosophy centered on connection, energy and interdependence. The spiral structure of the cords alludes to natural systems such as DNA, suggesting a continuous exchange between earth, sky, and living beings. This layered symbolism, combined with its architectural scale, allows the 'Garbo' lamp to function both as a singular sculptural light or as a subtle room divider. The piece reflects a moment in the 1970s when Italian manufacturers increasingly collaborated with Japanese designers.

name: Ceiling lamp designed by Bent Karlby for LYFA
description: This pendant lamp belongs to the Mosaik series designed by Bent Karlby, a collection built around a clear geometric idea and a modular approach to form. When introduced, the Mosaik series stood out for its playful use of colour and its departure from more restrained post-war lighting. The nature of the design meant that the same components could be adapted across pendant, wall, table and floor lamps, highlighting Karlby’s interest in versatility. Bent Karlby was one of Denmark’s most prolific lighting designers and worked closely with LYFA from the 1940s onward. While he is often associated with softly diffused light and organic silhouettes, his later work increasingly explored geometric forms and bold colour combinations. The Mosaik series reflects this shift, combining clarity of shape with a lively, modern character that remains distinctive within Scandinavian lighting design.
